paragraphs: Contextual language models represent a word differently depending on its surrounding sentence. This paper investigates whether those representations encode social biases involving gender, race, and intersecting identities. It examines models including BERT and GPT-2, asking how bias should be measured when a word’s representation changes with context.

The authors propose measuring bias at the contextual word level. This preserves information about how a particular context affects a word, while avoiding confounding effects that can make whole-sentence representations underestimate bias. The choice of measurement level therefore matters: combining information into a sentence representation can conceal associations visible in individual contextualized words.

The study finds corpus-level evidence of bias and varying evidence across embedding association tests. It reports strong encoding of racial bias and amplified bias for intersectional minorities beyond their constituent minority identities. Contextual word measurements also reveal biases missed at the sentence level. These findings support evaluating contextual representations directly, rather than assuming improved language-task performance or sentence-level testing establishes their fairness.
neurips-2019-assessing-social-and-inters.tldr: Measuring bias in contextualized words reveals racial and intersectional biases that whole-sentence measurements can miss.

paragraphs: Sketch-and-solve regression first compresses data through a random projection, then fits a regression model to the compressed version. This paper studies the statistical accuracy lost through that compression when data come from a linear model. Its goal is to distinguish projection methods more precisely than earlier statistical and computational analyses allowed.

The authors use an asymptotic setting in which both the number of observations and the number of features grow without bound. Within that framework, they derive limiting accuracy losses for estimating regression parameters and predicting test data. Considering both quantities separates recovering the underlying model from using it to make predictions.

The analysis distinguishes popular sketching methods and shows an advantage for the Subsampled Randomized Hadamard Transform over Gaussian projections in the studied setting. Experiments on real and synthetic data verify the theoretical results. The work also develops random matrix techniques for analyzing the Hadamard-based method. Its central contribution is a finer account of how the choice of compression affects regression accuracy.
neurips-2019-asymptotics-for-sketching-i.tldr: An asymptotic analysis distinguishes regression sketching methods and shows lower accuracy loss for SRHT than Gaussian projections.

paragraphs: This paper examines a representational restriction of Neural Ordinary Differential Equations, or Neural ODEs. The authors show that the representations these models learn preserve the topology of the input space. Topology concerns structural relationships in a space, so preserving it places constraints on the transformations a model can express.

The authors prove that this restriction means some functions cannot be represented by Neural ODEs. This is an expressiveness result: the issue concerns which functions belong to the model’s repertoire, beyond how successfully a particular training procedure fits data. The paper introduces Augmented Neural ODEs to address these representational limitations and establishes that they are more expressive.

The reported experiments also favor the augmented models on stability, generalization, and computational cost relative to Neural ODEs. Those practical advantages are empirical findings, whereas the original representational restriction is proved. Together, the results connect a mathematical constraint on a model family with an architectural response that also performs better in the authors’ empirical comparisons.
neurips-2019-augmented-neural-odes-11f1c.tldr: Augmented Neural ODEs address proven expressiveness limits of Neural ODEs and empirically improve stability, generalization, and computational cost.

paragraphs: The paper studies multi-armed bandits under a restriction that decisions must be organized into a small number of batches. A bandit policy must learn which options are rewarding while choosing among them. Batching constrains that learning process, making the relationship between available options, feedback opportunities, and regret an important theoretical question.

Earlier work had characterized minimax regret for the two-option stochastic problem. This paper addresses the multi-option case and asks whether choosing batch sizes adaptively can reduce regret. The authors introduce BaSE, a batched successive elimination policy, and prove regret guarantees that are rate-optimal up to logarithmic factors.

The accompanying lower bounds match those guarantees at that level of precision, even when batch sizes may be chosen adaptively. Consequently, adaptive batching does not bypass the fundamental regret limits established by the analysis. The contribution combines an achievable policy with a characterization of what any policy can accomplish, clarifying the statistical cost of learning through a limited number of batches.
neurips-2019-batched-multi-armed-bandits.tldr: BaSE achieves optimal batched multi-armed bandit regret rates up to logarithmic factors, with lower bounds that also cover adaptive batch sizes.

paragraphs: Compressed sensing MRI seeks to accelerate imaging by reconstructing clear images from undersampled measurements in k-space. Taking fewer measurements creates a reconstruction challenge: the system must remove aliasing while respecting the data actually collected. This paper proposes a Cascaded Dilated Dense Network, or CDDN, for that task.

The network restores images through successive subnetworks using dense blocks and residual connections. Dilated convolutions expand the area each operation can draw information from without increasing the number of network parameters. This combines stepwise image refinement with access to a broader spatial context, addressing reconstruction through both network structure and repeated processing.

After each subnetwork, a two-step data-consistency operation works in k-space. The method converts the complex output of the first consistency operation into a real-valued image, then replaces sampled k-space data again. This explicitly reconnects learned reconstruction with observed measurements. The authors report state-of-the-art results in extensive experiments for the combined CDDN and two-step consistency method.
neurips-2019-cascaded-dilated-dense-netw.tldr: CDDN combines staged image refinement, dilated convolutions, and two-step measurement consistency for state-of-the-art experimental MRI reconstruction.

paragraphs: Regularization usually penalizes model complexity to reduce overfitting. This paper argues that it can sometimes also improve causal modeling when an unobserved variable influences both predictors and the target. Such confounding can make a predictive relationship differ from the causal influence one wants to estimate.

The authors first study a linear setting with multidimensional predictors and an unobserved multidimensional common cause. In their model, retaining Ridge or Lasso penalties can reduce confounding even in the population limit, where finite-data overfitting is no longer the explanation. They connect this behavior to an analogy between confounding and overfitting, and choose penalty strength by estimating confounding rather than using the usual cross-validation approach.

That procedure yields reasonable results on simulated and real data. The paper also gives a causal generalization bound for interpreting nonlinear regression causally. The bound depends on the authors’ particular confounding model and on restricting the richness of the function class. These qualifications make regularization a conditional aid to causal inference, rather than a general solution to hidden confounding.
neurips-2019-causal-regularization-e132f.tldr: Under a particular confounding model, regularization can reduce causal estimation error even when finite-sample overfitting is absent.

paragraphs: Human bodies have a natural left-right mirroring structure. Chirality Nets build this structure into neural networks through equivariance to a chirality transform. Equivariance means that transforming the input produces the corresponding transformation of the output, making the network’s response consistent with the symmetry being modeled.

The authors construct and prove this property for variants of familiar components, including fully connected and convolutional layers, batch normalization, and LSTM and GRU cells. Their construction uses parameter sharing together with odd and even symmetry. Encoding these relationships in the components reduces computation and supports more efficient use of training data.

The paper evaluates the networks on video-based 3D pose estimation, 2D pose forecasting, and skeleton-based activity recognition. It reports results that achieve or match the state of the art, with larger gains when datasets or available training data are small. The findings suggest that explicitly representing the body’s symmetry can be particularly useful when examples alone provide limited opportunity to learn it.
neurips-2019-chirality-nets-for-human-po.tldr: Chirality Nets encode left-right symmetry in network layers, improving data efficiency and matching or achieving state-of-the-art pose-related results.

paragraphs: This paper develops a deep multi-state Dynamic Recurrent Neural Network for predicting computer cursor movement from neural recordings. The input is wavelet-based neural features derived from open-loop posterior parietal cortex data from a human subject. The design balances prediction performance, robustness, and memory demands for possible future hardware implementation.

The network feeds its own predictions back into its input. Scheduled sampling addresses the distribution mismatch between ground-truth values and model predictions, supporting the use of that feedback. The authors also configure a small network with a short input history, reducing how much data must be buffered and how often memory must be accessed.

Those memory choices lower expected power consumption in a neural network accelerator; the abstract presents this as an anticipated hardware benefit. On single-day and multi-day recordings spanning 43 days, average prediction performance surpasses other state-of-the-art methods in the literature. The results indicate potential for modeling nonlinear neural-to-movement relationships robustly, with the reported evidence grounded in the described subject’s recordings.
neurips-2019-deep-multi-state-dynamic-re.tldr: A compact recurrent network predicts cursor movement from neural features while balancing accuracy, robustness, and anticipated hardware efficiency.

paragraphs: Stochastic compositional optimization concerns objectives formed by composing two expectations of random functions. This nested structure makes optimization harder than in an ordinary stochastic objective. The paper addresses the general smooth, nonconvex setting, motivated by applications such as reinforcement learning and portfolio management.

The authors develop SARAH-Compositional using the idea of stochastic recursive gradient descent. They analyze incremental first-order oracle complexity, which measures the amount of first-order information an algorithm requires. In the finite-sum setting, they prove an upper bound of O((n+m)^(1/2) ε^(-2)); in the online setting, the bound is O(ε^(-3)). These are separate guarantees for two ways of accessing stochastic objectives.

The abstract identifies these bounds as the best known first-order oracle complexity results for nonconvex stochastic compositional optimization. It also reports numerical experiments supporting the algorithm’s superior performance and the theory. The contribution therefore combines an optimization method with explicit efficiency guarantees, while keeping the claim tied to smooth nonconvex compositional problems and the stated oracle measure.
neurips-2019-efficient-smooth-non-convex.tldr: SARAH-Compositional provides best-known stated first-order oracle complexity bounds for smooth nonconvex stochastic compositional optimization.

paragraphs: Graph covering problems arise when an intervention must reach people or locations connected through a network. This paper studies robust covering under uncertainty, motivated by social-network suicide prevention and landslide risk management. It finds that existing robust covering algorithms can produce biased coverage when fairness is absent from the optimization problem.

The authors introduce a formulation with group fairness constraints and a tractable approximation scheme intended for real-world instances. Fairness becomes an explicit requirement alongside coverage and robustness. They also analyze the price of group fairness: the cost associated with imposing fairness requirements. Their analysis shows that uncertainty can increase this price, linking equitable allocation to how unpredictable deployment conditions are.

Experiments on several real-world social networks show competitive overall node coverage alongside significantly improved group fairness compared with state-of-the-art methods. The result demonstrates that addressing biased coverage need not eliminate useful coverage performance in the tested settings. It also shows why uncertainty and fairness deserve joint analysis when designing network-based interventions.
neurips-2019-exploring-algorithmic-fairn.tldr: Fairness-constrained robust graph covering improves group equity while retaining competitive coverage, and uncertainty can increase the cost of fairness.

paragraphs: Natural gradient descent can help optimization when the objective has difficult curvature, but its convergence in nonlinear neural networks has been less understood. This paper analyzes convergence to a global optimum for nonlinear networks trained with squared error, providing conditions under which that behavior is guaranteed.

The two conditions concern the network’s Jacobian, which describes how outputs on the training examples change with the parameters. It must have full row rank and remain stable under small perturbations around initialization. The authors prove that both conditions hold throughout training for two-layer ReLU networks under assumptions of nondegenerate inputs and sufficient overparameterization.

The analysis also extends to more general loss functions with similar convergence behavior. Additionally, the authors establish global-minimum convergence for K-FAC, an approximate natural gradient method, under the same assumptions. The significance is a theoretical connection between network structure, local output sensitivity, and successful optimization. These are conditional guarantees, rather than claims that natural gradient or K-FAC globally solves every neural-network training problem.
neurips-2019-fast-convergence-of-natural.tldr: The paper gives sufficient Jacobian conditions for global convergence of natural gradient and proves relevant guarantees for overparameterized two-layer ReLU networks.

paragraphs: Training related tasks together can improve generalization, but the benefit depends on the relationship between those tasks. This paper develops an analytic theory of how generalization evolves in deep neural classifiers. It covers both single-task and multitask training with softmax outputs and cross-entropy loss, extending a line of analysis largely focused on regression.

The authors adapt methods from the statistical physics of disordered systems to study nonlinear learning dynamics. Their treatment accounts for finite datasets and correlations between outputs that arise during training. They compare the theoretical results with a comprehensive collection of numerical experiments to assess how well the analysis describes observed behavior.

The analysis supports the idea that task noise and alignment between input features determine multitask performance. Highly related, clean tasks can benefit one another, whereas unrelated, clean tasks can harm individual-task performance. This explains why adding another task is not automatically useful: even clean supervision can be detrimental when the tasks’ features do not align in a helpful way.
neurips-2019-generalization-in-multitask.tldr: A statistical-physics analysis links multitask classifier generalization to task noise and feature alignment, explaining both benefits and detrimental interactions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how overparameterized shallow ReLU networks learn to interpolate data with one-dimensional inputs using least squares. Its theoretical and empirical analysis focuses on the trajectory of learning and the shapes of the resulting functions. This makes initialization important as a determinant of the solution’s structure, beyond merely providing starting parameter values.

The authors show that the network’s gradient dynamics are determined by gradient flow in a nonredundant representation of the network function. They identify conditions for two learning regimes, called kernel and adaptive. Which regime appears depends on relative initialization magnitudes across layers and on how initialization coefficients behave as network width becomes large.

In the kernel regime, learning produces smooth interpolants that minimize curvature; uniform initializations lead to cubic splines. The adaptive regime instead favors linear splines whose knots cluster at sample locations. These findings connect initialization choices to different forms of interpolation, showing how the same broad network family can favor either smooth curvature-minimizing fits or adaptively positioned piecewise-linear structure.
neurips-2019-gradient-dynamics-of-shallo.tldr: Initialization determines whether shallow one-dimensional ReLU networks learn smooth kernel-regime interpolants or adaptive linear splines.

paragraphs: Graph Normalizing Flows introduces a reversible graph neural network for both prediction and generation. The supervised part addresses a practical scaling problem: graph models must manage memory as graph size increases. The authors report predictive performance similar to message passing neural networks while using significantly less memory.

That smaller memory footprint allows the model to scale to larger graphs. For unsupervised learning, the authors combine the flow model with a new graph autoencoder to generate graph structures. The resulting generative model is permutation-invariant, so arbitrary ordering of graph elements does not define the modeled structure.

The model generates an entire graph in one feed-forward pass. This organization is better suited to parallel computing architectures than the autoregressive models used for comparison, while achieving competitive results. The paper thus connects two computational advantages to graph learning: reduced memory for supervised prediction and whole-graph generation that supports parallel execution. Its reported comparisons establish similar or competitive performance alongside these architectural benefits.
neurips-2019-graph-normalizing-flows-638.tldr: Reversible graph networks reduce prediction memory requirements and support competitive, permutation-invariant graph generation in a single feed-forward pass.

paragraphs: Training a denoising model often depends on reference data that are costly or impossible to acquire. This paper presents a method that learns from an unorganized collection of corrupted images. It requires neither clean reference images nor explicit pairs of noisy images, broadening the circumstances in which denoising models can be trained.

The method builds on networks with a blind spot in their receptive field. This design leaves part of the input unavailable to the corresponding prediction, supporting training without a clean target image. The paper improves both image quality and training efficiency within this approach, addressing the usefulness of the reconstructed images as well as the cost of learning.

The reported quality matches state-of-the-art neural denoisers for independent, identically distributed additive Gaussian noise. Performance is somewhat behind for Poisson and impulse noise. The method also successfully handles cases where noise parameters vary or are unknown in training and evaluation data. These findings support reference-free training while preserving the distinctions between the tested noise settings.
neurips-2019-high-quality-self-supervise.tldr: Blind-spot denoisers learn from unpaired corrupted images and match state-of-the-art quality for i.i.d. additive Gaussian noise.

paragraphs: Many network relationships involve groups rather than pairs. Co-authorship, co-citation, and email communication motivate using hypergraphs, which can represent relationships involving multiple vertices together. This paper asks how graph convolutional learning can be applied to that richer structure, particularly when only some vertices have known labels.

The authors propose HyperGCN for semi-supervised learning on attributed hypergraphs. The task is to assign labels to initially unlabeled vertices, using a representation that includes vertex attributes and group relationships. The approach is motivated by the effectiveness of graph convolutional networks for the corresponding learning problem on ordinary graphs.

The paper also shows how HyperGCN can serve as a learning-based approach to combinatorial optimization on NP-hard hypergraph problems. Detailed experiments on real-world hypergraphs demonstrate its effectiveness, and the authors provide source code to support reproducibility. The contribution extends the use of graph convolutional learning to settings where group structure matters, covering both label prediction and a further role in difficult optimization problems.
neurips-2019-hypergcn-a-new-method-for-t.tldr: HyperGCN applies graph convolutional learning to attributed hypergraphs for semi-supervised labeling and learning-based combinatorial optimization.

paragraphs: Hidden common causes make causal discovery harder because observed variables can share influences that are not directly measured. The paper connects causal discovery methods in this setting to overcomplete independent component analysis, or OICA. Existing OICA methods often impose strong distributional assumptions and require expensive inference through expectation maximization.

The proposed Likelihood-Free Overcomplete ICA method estimates the mixing matrix directly through backpropagation. It does so without explicit assumptions about the density functions of the independent components. This addresses both the risk of imposing unsuitable parametric distributions and the computational burden of inferring posterior distributions for those components.

The authors demonstrate efficiency and efficacy on two causal discovery tasks using synthetic and real data. They argue that the computational improvement makes several causal discovery procedures more practical. The contribution is therefore a more flexible and efficient component-estimation method for these procedures. Avoiding explicit density assumptions should be understood in that specific sense; the method remains an independent-component approach connected to the causal settings under study.
neurips-2019-likelihood-free-overcomplet.tldr: LFOICA directly learns mixing matrices without explicit component-density assumptions, improving the practicality of causal discovery with hidden common causes.

paragraphs: A classifier can confidently misidentify inputs that differ from its training distribution. This paper studies detecting such inputs, motivated by identifying bacteria from genomic sequences. A useful system should recognize when sequences come from previously unseen bacteria rather than confidently assigning them to familiar categories.

The authors introduce a genomics dataset for out-of-distribution detection and investigate detection with deep generative models. They observe that raw likelihood is strongly influenced by population-level background statistics. Those statistics can confound the score, making likelihood a misleading signal of whether an input belongs to the intended distribution. Their likelihood-ratio method corrects for these background effects.

On the genomics benchmark, the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art detection performance compared with existing approaches. Applying it to generative image models also significantly improves detection, demonstrating usefulness beyond the motivating genomic setting. The findings emphasize that a model’s likelihood score can mix relevant distributional evidence with background regularities, and that accounting for this distinction can improve detection of unfamiliar inputs.
neurips-2019-likelihood-ratios-for-out-o.tldr: Likelihood ratios correct confounding background statistics and improve out-of-distribution detection for genomic sequences and images.

paragraphs: Approximate nearest-neighbor search helps find similar objects in high-dimensional datasets without exhaustively comparing every pair. This paper develops locality-sensitive hashing methods for cases where similarity is measured between probability distributions. It focuses on f-divergences and extends the treatment to mutual information loss.

The authors provide a general framework for constructing hashing schemes for f-divergence distance functions. Within it, they develop schemes for generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence and triangular discrimination. They also prove a two-sided approximation of generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence using Hellinger distance, giving a controlled relationship between two ways of comparing distributions.

A second contribution addresses Krein kernels, which can be expressed as the difference of two positive definite kernels. The authors reduce designing a hashing scheme for such a kernel to maximum inner product search. They illustrate this reduction with mutual information loss, a quantity relevant to applications including model compression. Together, these results connect distribution-based comparisons to established search machinery through explicit mathematical constructions and approximation results.
neurips-2019-locality-sensitive-hashing-.tldr: The paper develops hashing frameworks for distribution divergences and reduces certain kernel-based search problems to maximum inner product search.

paragraphs: Flow-based generative models offer tractable exact likelihood computation and latent-variable inference, alongside efficient training and sampling. However, the paper identifies a substantial density-estimation gap between these models and leading autoregressive approaches. MaCow is designed to improve that aspect of flow modeling while retaining useful computational properties.

The proposed architecture uses masked convolutions with local connectivity restricted to a small kernel. This makes the pattern of connections a central architectural choice. The authors report that the resulting generative flow supports fast, stable training and efficient sampling, connecting its constrained local structure with practical computation.

On standard image benchmarks, MaCow significantly improves density estimation over Glow and substantially narrows the gap to autoregressive models. The claim is an improvement and a narrowing of that gap, rather than elimination of it. The paper’s contribution is a simple flow architecture that brings better density modeling together with the training and sampling advantages that motivate this model family.
neurips-2019-macow-masked-convolutional-.tldr: MaCow uses locally masked convolutions to improve flow-based image density estimation while retaining fast training and efficient sampling.

paragraphs: Selecting a classification metric amounts to deciding what kinds of performance a user values. Those preferences may be implicit, making it difficult to choose a metric directly. This paper studies metric elicitation: a principled process for finding a performance measure that reflects the user’s preferences.

The authors extend this framework from binary classification to classification with multiple classes. Their strategies use only relative preference feedback. In practical terms, this means learning from judgments about which alternative is preferred, rather than requiring the user to specify the desired metric outright. The contribution concerns how evaluation criteria are selected for multiclass problems.

The paper also shows robustness to finite-sample effects and noisy feedback. These address two distinct sources of uncertainty: limited data used to assess performance and imperfect preference information from the user. The stated result supports eliciting metrics without assuming unlimited data or perfectly reliable feedback. Its significance is to make preference-based metric selection applicable beyond two-class problems while accounting for uncertainty in the information it receives.
neurips-2019-multiclass-performance-metr.tldr: The paper extends preference-based performance metric elicitation to multiclass classification with robustness to limited data and noisy feedback.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether an artificial neural network can develop through growth and self-organization instead of having its full architecture specified by hand. The authors propose a biologically inspired algorithm that starts from a single cell and grows a functional layered network, organizing connections into retinotopic pooling layers.

The approach draws inspiration from early visual-system wiring before animals open their eyes. Its key ingredients are spontaneous activity waves across the first layer and a local learning rule in the second layer that learns the underlying activity pattern. These mechanisms organize connections using internally emerging activity rather than requiring each connection to be individually designed.

The algorithm accommodates varied input-layer geometries, tolerates malfunctioning first-layer units, and grows pooling structures with different sizes and shapes. Networks grown from a single unit perform as well as handcrafted networks on MNIST. The work presents a primitive developmental procedure for constructing layered networks, with evidence that the resulting self-organized structures can support useful computation.
neurips-2019-neural-networks-grown-and-s.tldr: A biologically inspired growth algorithm uses spontaneous activity and local learning to build functional networks that match handcrafted networks on MNIST.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimizers commonly discard gradients after using them once. Reusing them can reduce variance, but older gradients become stale as parameters change, especially in online optimization. This paper proposes implicit gradient transport, or IGT, to correct that mismatch and make past gradient information useful at the current iterate.

IGT transforms previously computed gradients to account for the current parameters without explicitly using the Hessian. The authors report reductions in both variance and bias over time. Because IGT supplies a gradient estimate, it can replace that part of established optimizers such as heavy ball or Adam, allowing the reuse mechanism to fit into familiar update methods.

Experiments show state-of-the-art results across a wide range of architectures and benchmarks. The paper also proves an optimal asymptotic convergence rate for online stochastic optimization in the restricted case where all component functions have equal Hessians. The practical evidence therefore spans multiple tested settings, while the strongest theoretical rate guarantee depends on a specific shared-curvature condition.
neurips-2019-reducing-the-variance-in-on.tldr: Implicit gradient transport reuses past gradients with a staleness correction, improving optimization empirically and achieving an optimal asymptotic rate under equal component Hessians.

paragraphs: Layer normalization can stabilize neural-network training, but its computational overhead can slow the underlying model, particularly recurrent networks. This paper investigates whether its recentering behavior is necessary. The authors hypothesize that it can be removed while keeping the useful effects of controlling scale.

They propose RMSNorm, which normalizes summed inputs using their root mean square. The method retains rescaling invariance and provides implicit learning-rate adaptation while requiring simpler computation than LayerNorm. A further variant, partial RMSNorm, estimates the root mean square from only a percentage of the summed inputs, preserving those stated properties.

Experiments across several tasks and network architectures show performance comparable to LayerNorm with running-time reductions ranging from 7% to 64%, depending on the model. These results support the proposed simplification in the evaluated settings. The contribution separates two roles bundled into LayerNorm and shows that retaining scale normalization alone can offer a favorable performance-and-runtime trade-off without requiring the full original computation.
neurips-2019-root-mean-square-layer-norm.tldr: RMSNorm removes LayerNorm’s recentering operation while achieving comparable experimental performance and reducing runtime by 7%–64% across tested models.

paragraphs: Visual commonsense reasoning asks a model both to answer a question about an image and to justify the answer. This paper examines whether a complicated baseline is necessary for strong performance on that task. The motivation includes concern that apparent reasoning success can reflect dataset biases rather than the intended ability.

The authors simplify the existing baseline through ablation and pruning, obtaining better performance with half as many trainable parameters. They then improve this simpler model by associating visual features with attributes and strengthening text-to-image grounding. These additions emphasize the information available about visual content and how language is connected to it.

The resulting TAB-VCR model improves over the previous state of the art by 5.3 percentage points on question answering, 4.4 on answer justification, and 6.5 on holistic VCR. These benchmark gains show that architectural simplification can coexist with improved performance. They also highlight the value of richer visual attributes and better grounding within the proposed simpler baseline.
neurips-2019-tab-vcr-tags-and-attributes.tldr: TAB-VCR improves visual commonsense reasoning with a simpler baseline, visual attributes, and better text-to-image grounding.
